passage: On the first of January, Madhuri wrote "Be healthier" on the fridge whiteboard in big green letters. Gurpreet, her flatmate, asked what that meant. "Everything," Madhuri said. "Less fried stuff, more movement, better sleep." The first week went well because she was still thinking about it every morning. Then the office moved her to the late shift, and the bus home reached after ten. Some nights she remembered the board; most nights she was too tired to decide anything and ordered the same rolls from the stall downstairs. By the second week of February the green letters had faded under a shopping list. Gurpreet asked, gently, "When were you going to do it?" Madhuri opened her mouth, then laughed. "I never actually said when."

qa.q: What did Madhuri write on the fridge whiteboard on the first of January?
qa.a: "Be healthier," in big green letters.

qa.q: Why did the resolution feel strong to Madhuri at first?
qa.a: In the first week she was still thinking about it every morning, so the goal felt alive; she had not yet seen that it depended on remembering and having energy.

qa.q: Once the late shift began, what choice could have kept the goal alive?
qa.a: Tying one concrete action to a fixed moment in the new routine, such as a short walk from the bus stop before going upstairs, so nothing depends on deciding while tired.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see the resolution by February?
qa.a: Gurpreet watches the words fade under a shopping list and asks kindly, not critically, when it was meant to happen, which helps Madhuri spot the missing piece.

grounding: An adult makes a broad health resolution with no when or how, and it slips once tiredness and a new shift take over.

passage: "This is my year," Kishore announced at the office lunch table in Pune, spooning up dal. "Fitter, calmer, no more late-night scrolling." Gurleen, sitting across, asked which days he'd exercise. Kishore waved a hand. "Whenever I get time. I'll feel it." In January he climbed the stairs to the fourth floor instead of taking the lift, on the days he remembered. He bought a skipping rope and kept it in the car. By the end of the month the stairs happened only when the lift was broken, and the rope had slid under the car seat next to a tiffin lid. One evening in February, stuck in traffic, he found the rope while hunting for his charger and stared at it for a long time.

qa.q: Where did Kishore find the skipping rope in February?
qa.a: Under the car seat next to a tiffin lid, while hunting for his charger in traffic.

qa.q: What might Kishore have been thinking as he stared at the rope?
qa.a: He probably felt a pang of disappointment, seeing that the promise he made so confidently in January had quietly faded even though he never decided to drop it.

qa.q: Where did Kishore's plan go wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: "Whenever I get time" left every action to memory and mood; choosing set days and a cue, like taking the stairs every time he arrives at the office, would make it automatic.

qa.q: Why might Gurleen have asked which days?
qa.a: Gurleen seems to sense that a goal with no time attached rarely survives busy weeks, and the question was a light nudge to make it concrete.

grounding: An adult's vague resolution to get fit, with no set days or cues, drifts away by February.

passage:
"Didi, see this." Ankita held up her phone: a New Year post she had shared, "Healthier me, starting now."
Jyoti smiled. "Nice. What's the plan?"
"Just, you know, eat better, walk more. Be good."
"When's the walk?"
"Whenever. Mornings, maybe. I'll see how I feel."
Six weeks later, Jyoti found her on the sofa at eleven at night, eating chips from the packet.
"Ankita, how's the walking going?"
"Don't." Ankita pulled a cushion over her face. "I went on the fourth and the fifth. Then that deadline came, then it rained, then I just forgot it existed."
"Did you ever pick a time?"
A long pause. "No. I kept waiting to feel like it."
"Nobody feels like it at six in the morning."
"So I'm lazy?"
"No. You just left it to your mood."

qa.q: On which dates did Ankita actually go walking?
qa.a: On the fourth and the fifth.

qa.q: Why does Ankita pull a cushion over her face when Jyoti asks about the walking?
qa.a: She feels embarrassed that the plan she announced so happily has faded, and she worries it means she is lazy.

qa.q: What choice would change Ankita's next attempt?
qa.a: Picking a set time and a cue, such as walking straight after her morning tea, instead of waiting to feel like it.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see Ankita's slipping resolution?
qa.a: As her older sister, Jyoti doesn't see laziness; she notices the plan never had a time, so it depended on mood, and says so kindly.

grounding: A vague 'eat better, walk more' resolution with no time or trigger fades within weeks.

passage: I'm Sarita, and last New Year's Eve I told my flatmate Himani, very grandly, "This year I'm getting healthy." I never said what that meant. I think I pictured a new version of me who simply woke up wanting salad. For about two weeks I felt it. I walked a bit, skipped some biscuits, drank more water when I remembered. Then a big audit came at work. I stayed late, ate whatever the canteen had, and walking became something I'd do "when things settle". By February I was back to my old evenings exactly, and I hadn't even noticed the day it slipped. In March Himani asked how the healthy year was going. I laughed, but it stung. There had never been a when or a how, only a mood.

qa.q: What did Sarita tell Himani on New Year's Eve?
qa.a: Sarita said, 'This year I'm getting healthy.'

qa.q: Why did the resolution feel like it was working for Sarita in the first two weeks?
qa.a: The New Year mood carried it; Sarita felt motivated and still remembered the goal, so a concrete plan didn't seem necessary.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Sarita try instead?
qa.a: Nothing tied the goal to a time or cue, so the audit pushed it aside; Sarita could pick one action linked to a moment, like a walk straight after getting home on set days.

qa.q: What might Himani have noticed before asking in March?
qa.a: Himani had probably seen the old evenings return and asked as a gentle check-in, perhaps not realising the laugh covered a sting.

grounding: An adult makes a vague resolution to get healthy with no timing or method and slides back to old habits by February.

passage:
Instructor's note, Saturday yoga, Malleswaram community hall. Rashmi, 20 February.
Jeevan signed up on 2 January, full of energy. When I asked what he wanted, he said, "To be healthier, generally. Better food, more movement, all of it." I asked which days he'd come. "Whenever I can. I'll just feel it." He came three Saturdays running. Then his sister's wedding preparations started, then a work trip, and I haven't seen him since the last week of January. Today I met him at the vegetable stall. He said, a bit sheepishly, that he was "back to the old routine" and didn't know when it happened. Next time someone joins, I'll ask for one fixed class and what comes right before it. "Whenever" seems to depend on how the week feels.

qa.q: How many Saturdays did Jeevan come before he stopped?
qa.a: He came three Saturdays running.

qa.q: What does Jeevan's sheepishness at the vegetable stall suggest?
qa.a: He seems embarrassed; he still cares about the goal and hadn't noticed it slipping away, so meeting Rashmi brought it back to mind.

qa.q: What will Rashmi ask future joiners, and why might it help?
qa.a: One fixed class and what comes right before it; a set time and cue do the remembering, so the plan doesn't depend on how the week feels.

qa.q: How does Rashmi see Jeevan's drop-off?
qa.a: Rashmi doesn't treat it as laziness; the note suggests 'whenever' left Jeevan nothing to hold on to once the wedding and the work trip arrived.

grounding: A yoga instructor notes an adult whose general wish to be healthier, with no set time, faded by February.
